q: At what diameter is repair of an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm generally considered?
why: Surgery is generally considered once the diameter exceeds 5.5 cm, or if it grows more than about 1 cm a year. Rupture risk is under 1% a year below 4.5 cm.

q: What ACT target is used after heparin during EVAR?
why: Around 5,000 units heparin after femoral exposure, targeting an ACT of 200–250 s.

q: Which endoleak types generally need intervention?
why: Types 1 (attachment sites), 3 (graft defect) and 5 (endotension) usually need intervention; types 2 (branch filling) and 4 (porosity) are often watched.

q: What did the EVAR-2 trial show?
o: EVAR improves survival in patients unfit for open repair
No survival benefit of EVAR over no intervention in patients unfit for open repair
EVAR is better than open repair in all patients
Open repair has more long-term complications
why: EVAR-2 found no survival benefit in patients unfit for open repair. NICE notes EVAR has higher long-term complication rates and needs lifelong surveillance.

q: According to the IMPROVE trial, which factor in ruptured AAA correlated with 30-day mortality?
why: IMPROVE found comparable outcomes between open and endovascular-first strategies; mortality correlated with the lowest systolic BP, and local anaesthesia was associated with lower mortality.

q: Two days after EVAR, a patient has a fever, raised white cell count and CRP, with no source of infection. What is the most likely cause?
why: Post-implantation syndrome is a mild, self-limiting reaction to the graft material, lasting 2–10 days.

q: What is the main anaesthetic concern with fenestrated or branched ("complex") EVAR compared with standard EVAR?
o: Longer procedure, more contrast and usually GA, with more risk of AKI
why: Complex EVAR usually needs GA, a 4–6 unit crossmatch, more contrast (renal risk) and HDU/ICU care.

q: Which aortic aneurysm is the most extensive in the Crawford classification of thoracoabdominal aneurysms?
why: Type II runs from below the left subclavian to below the renal arteries; it is the most extensive.

q: In the UK AAA screening programme, which threshold triggers referral for CT?
why: Ultrasound screening refers men over 55 mm (women over 50 mm) for CT. The UK programme screens men; aneurysms in women and smokers carry higher rupture risk.

q: Which drugs are usually stopped before EVAR to protect renal function?
why: Stop NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors before contrast; optimise comorbidities and consider CPET for risk.
